prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A Creole boy from the West Indies brought, To be in European learning taught, Some years before to Westminster he went, To a Preparatory school was sent. When from his artless tale the mistress found The child had not one friend on English ground, She ev’n as if she his own mother were, Made the dark Indian her particular care. Oft on her favourite’s future lot she thought; To know the bent of his young mind she sought, For much the kind preceptress wished to find To what profession he was most inclined, That where his genius led they might him train; For nature’s kindly bent she held not vain. But vain her efforts to explore his will; The frequent question he evaded still; Till on a day at length he to her came, Joy sparkling in his eyes; and said, the same Trade he would be those boys of colour were, Who danced so happy in the open air. It was a troop of chimney-sweeping boys, With wooden music and obstreperous noise, In tarnish’d finery and grotesque array, Were dancing in the streets the first of May.

Across the vast expanse of the Atlantic, a young Creole boy was uprooted from the warm, sun-drenched shores of the West Indies and brought to the damp, unfamiliar climate of England. His family had sent him far from home to attend a prestigious preparatory school, determined that he should receive a proper European education. Adjusting to this cold, regimented new world was daunting for the young child, who found himself completely isolated in a foreign land.

Recognizing the boy’s profound solitude, the school’s headmistress took a special interest in his well-being. She saw a vulnerable child who had neither friends nor family anywhere in the country to offer him comfort. Moved by compassion, the kindly woman effectively adopted the boy into her heart, surrounding him with warm maternal care and ensuring he never felt entirely abandoned. 

As time passed, the schoolmistress grew deeply invested in the boy's future. Driven by a desire to see him succeed in English society, she repeatedly tried to uncover his natural talents and interests. She would gently coax him into conversations about his dreams, hoping to identify a spark of ambition that could guide him toward a respectable profession—perhaps in law, medicine, or commerce. 

For a long time, the boy remained evasive. Whenever the topic of his future career arose, he would grow shy, offering vague answers or artfully steering the conversation elsewhere. His silence left the mistress wondering what truly lay in the heart of her young charge.

That mystery was unexpectedly solved on May Day. While looking out at the festive street celebrations, the boy witnessed a troupe of young chimney sweeps, their faces and arms thoroughly blackened with soot, dancing joyfully in the parade. To the child, their dark complexions and uninhibited happiness radiated a sense of familiar warmth and freedom that he had missed since leaving the West Indies. 

Overjoyed by the sight, the boy rushed to his guardian, his eyes bright with newfound enthusiasm. Bursting with genuine pride and certainty, he eagerly announced that he had finally discovered his life’s calling: he was going to become a chimney sweep.
outputs.L4:
Miss Penelope Vance was a woman of formidable purpose and relentless pedagogical zeal. As a schoolmistress in the sleepy, rain-drenched coastal town of East Sussex, she viewed the mind of a child not as a vessel to be filled, but as a complex puzzle waiting to be solved. Her greatest and most delicate project was young Leo, a seven-year-old Creole boy entrusted to her care following the tragic death of his merchant father. 

Leo was a child of luminous warmth, possessing dark, expressive eyes that seemed perpetually focused on something just beyond the parlor window. To Miss Vance, he was a bright gem cast against the grey canvas of English provincial life. Yet, his foreign origins and uncertain inheritance weighed heavily upon her conscience. She felt it her sacred duty to equip him for a respectable, self-sustaining future in a society that was rarely kind to outsiders.

To this end, Miss Vance embarked on a systematic campaign of vocational discovery. Day after day, as the kettle hummed upon the grate, she would sit Leo down at the heavy mahogany desk and subject him to earnest interrogations.

"Consider, Leo," she would say, her quill poised above a crisp sheet of parchment. "Every man is given a peculiar gift by Providence. Is your mind drawn to the precision of numbers? A clerkship in London, perhaps? Or do you feel a calling toward the natural sciences? We might cultivate an interest in botany."

Leo would shift uncomfortably in his stiff woolen trousers, his small hands tracing the carved wood of his chair. He tried valiantly to please her. When she suggested law, he nodded dutifully. When she posited the navy, he offered a weak smile. But his answers were always hollow, born of polite obedience rather than inner fire. He possessed no obvious inclination for ledger books, Latin declensions, or the dry rhetoric of sermons. Miss Vance’s ledger remained frustratingly blank, save for her neat, increasingly anxious marginal notes.

The breakthrough—if it could be called that—arrived on the first morning of May. 

The town, usually dreary, transformed into a riot of folk tradition. From the schoolhouse window, Leo watched the May Day procession wind its way down the cobblestone street. There were flower-laden maidens and fiddlers, but what captured the boy's absolute enchantment was the troupe of sweeps. 

In keeping with old English custom, the chimney sweeps had taken a holiday from their grimy toil. Dressed in fantastical rags adorned with bright ribbons, their faces blackened with chimney soot, they danced wildly through the streets. Among them was the *Jack-in-the-Green*, a walking bower of foliage and flowers, surrounded by soot-faced boys who leaped, spun, and clattered their brushes like castanets, collecting pennies from the laughing crowd. Leo was spellbound. He pressed his forehead against the glass, his eyes wide, his chest heaving with unadulterated delight at the rhythmic, chaotic explosion of color, sound, and movement.

Miss Vance observed his rapt expression with a surge of triumphant hope. At last, the spark had been struck. The boy had witnessed the grand drama of public life and found his inspiration. She decided to give him a few hours to ponder what he had seen before striking while the iron was hot.

That evening, over a supper of dry toast and tea, Miss Vance laid out her notebook once more. 

"Leo," she began, her voice brimming with encouraging warmth, "I saw how deeply moved you were by the morning’s spectacles. The grandeur of human effort, the harmony of community! Tell me, my dear boy, now that you have seen what lies out in the world—what is the true desire of your heart? What do you wish to become?"

Leo set down his teacup. For the first time since he had arrived in England, his posture was straight not out of discipline, but out of sheer, glowing enthusiasm. 

"I have made up my mind, Miss Vance," he declared, his voice ringing with absolute certainty. "I am going to be a sweep."

Miss Vance’s quill hovered in mid-air. A drop of black ink pooled on the clean page. "A... a sweep? A chimney sweep, Leo?"

"Yes!" Leo beamed, his hands gesturing wildly. "But not just the sweeping part. I shall be a *dancing* sweep! I will cover my face in the finest black soot and tie scarlet ribbons to my knees. I will carry my broom like a king's sword, and when May comes, I will dance in the middle of the street until the town gives me all their pennies!"

Miss Vance sat in stunned, paralyzed silence. 

In a single, joyful confession, the boy had demolished her grand blueprints for his future. She had envisioned him in high-collared coats, deliberating in law courts or managing shipping lines; he envisioned himself caked in creosote, twirling like a dervish for the amusement of passersby. All her lofty ambitions, her earnest theories on pedagogical uplift and social elevation, had collided head-on with the innocent, unburdened absurdity of a child’s imagination.

She looked at the boy, whose face was illuminated by the flickering hearth fire, so full of pure, uncalculating joy. The heavy burden of her responsibility suddenly felt both absurd and light. 

Slowly, Miss Vance dipped her pen in the inkwell. With a quiet sigh that was half-despair and half-amusement, she lowered the tip to the page. Beneath her long list of sensible professions—*Merchant, Scholar, Magistrate*—she carefully wrote, in her flawless copperplate script:

*May 1st: Expresses a keen interest in soot, ribbons, and street-dancing.*

She closed the book, looked at the young boy who was already drumming a merry May Day beat upon the table with his spoon, and realized that for tonight, at least, the future could wait.
outputs.L5:
Scattered across the turquoise expanse of the Caribbean Sea, the islands of the **West Indies** are far more than a tropical paradise of sun-drenched beaches and rustling palms. They are the cradle of a remarkable cultural alchemy: the **Creole** identity. To understand the West Indies is to understand the spirit of *Créolité*—a living, breathing tapestry woven from resilience, fusion, and artistic brilliance.

The story of the West Indies is one of collision and creation. Over centuries of trade, colonization, and migration, the archipelago became a crossroads of the world. Enslaved Africans, European settlers, Indigenous populations, and later, indentured laborers from South and East Asia were brought together on these isolated shores. Out of a complex and often painful history emerged a culture of profound adaptability. The term "Creole," originally used to describe those born in the New World, evolved into a symbol of a dynamic, blended heritage unique to the region.

Nowhere is this synthesis more vibrant than in the languages of the West Indies. As disparate groups sought ways to communicate, Creole languages were born. Whether it is the French-based Patois spoken in Haiti, Martinique, and Saint Lucia, or the English-influenced Creoles of Jamaica and Guyana, these mother tongues are far more than mere dialects. They are rich, expressive languages filled with proverbs, humor, and poetic rhythm—capturing the nuances of island life in ways colonial languages never could.

This creative synthesis extends into every corner of daily life in the West Indies. In the kitchen, Creole cuisine transforms simple, local ingredients into extraordinary feasts. African cooking techniques meet European culinary styles, elevated by East Indian spices and Indigenous crops. Dishes like callaloo, jerk seasoning, pelau, and saltfish fritters are savory odes to this shared history. 

Similarly, the region's music and dance carry the Creole heartbeat. The syncopated rhythms of West African drums merged with European melodies to give birth to calypso, reggae, zouk, and soca. These sounds do not merely entertain; they tell the stories of resistance, celebration, and everyday struggle.

Ultimately, the Creole heritage of the West Indies is a testament to the triumph of the human spirit. It demonstrates how people from vastly different origins can come together on small islands and create a brand-new, enduring world. In an increasingly interconnected global landscape, the Creole culture of the West Indies stands as a vibrant example of unity in diversity—a celebration of life forged in the warmth of the Caribbean sun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 19th-century narrative poem in rhyming couplets about a young Creole boy sent to school in England who decides he wants to become a chimney sweep after seeing them dance on May Day.
counterfactuals.output:
From islands where the fragrant orchids bloom,
Young Gabriel came to London’s heavy gloom.
A Creole child of warmth and golden skies,
With summer’s sunlight lingering in his eyes,
He left the palms and orange-scented breeze
To cross the wide and cold Atlantic seas.
His father deemed that English scholar-craft
Should tame the lad who once had sung and laughed.

In tailored cloth and collar folded neat,
He sat confined upon the scholar’s seat,
Where master’s ruler clattered on the board,
And dreary Latin paradigms were poured.
How cold the grey stone wall, how faint the sun!
How slow the dull and tedious hours run!
He missed the indigo, the parrot’s call,
The easy freedom of his father's hall.

Then came the merry First of May at last,
And through the town a sudden magic passed.
Fife, drum, and fiddle echoed down the street,
With leap and laugh of eager, hurrying feet.
The school was freed to view the grand parade,
Where leafy bowers in the lanes were made.
And high above the crowd there rose a frame
Of woven boughs, whence laughing voices came:
The Jack-in-the-Green, in emerald attire,
Who twirled as though his heels were struck with fire.

And who were those that danced around his knee,
With wilder grace than Gabriel e'er did see?
The little sweeps! Though blackened by the flue,
They wore bright crowns of hawthorn wet with dew.
With faces smudged in velvet soot and grime,
They beat their shovels in a rhythmic chime.
They twirled in ribbons, laughed without a care,
And tossed their tumbled locks of dusty hair.

To Gabriel's eyes, untaught in English woes,
They seemed like spirits where the night-wind blows—
Not tragic victims of the chimney-draft,
But kings of smoke who merrily leaped and laughed!
He saw them caper, light as fallen leaves,
Unbound by tutors or the schoolhouse eaves.
Their soot appeared like armor, rich and dark,
And in their dark eyes shone a vital spark.

No master checked their wild, untamed delight;
They danced in day, though painted like the night.
They roamed the roofs above the quiet town,
And from the clouds looked all the world adown.
Young Gabriel felt his heavy spirit rise;
A sudden fire burned within his eyes.

"Take back my books!" the Creole boy exclaimed,
"My fine silk coat, my collar neatly framed!
No more I'll weep for sunnier lands across,
Nor count these dreary grammar rules a loss.
I’ll take the scraper and the birch-twig broom,
And leap like shadows through the chimney room!
Let scholars seek what ancient sages spoke—
I’ll join the merry brotherhood of smoke!"
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Please generate a period-accurate Victorian style poem depicting a caring English schoolmistress trying to figure out the future ambition of a young West Indian student.
counterfactuals.output:
The rain taps cold upon the leaded glass,
The foggy winter twilight gathers slow;
I watch the smallest scholar of my class,
Whose quiet eyes preserve the sun's warm glow.
Far from the island where the citrus blooms,
And turquoise waters lap the coral strand,
He sits within these grey and chalk-dust rooms,
A gentle stranger in a chilly land.

"Come tell me, Master Edward," soft I speak,
And lay my hand upon his ink-stained slate,
"What calling in the wide world do you seek?
What path to tread when you are grown and great?
Would you command a vessel on the deep,
To sail beneath the constant Southern Cross?
Or watch where green, wild sugar-canes do sweep,
And tend the island fields through gain and loss?"

He lifts his gaze, so thoughtful and profound,
Toward the atlas pinned upon the wall;
He heeds no more the damp wind’s dreary sound,
Determined, though his stature is but small.
"I would not rule a ship, nor till the soil,"
He answers me, with shyly bright'ning eyes,
"For bookish wisdom is my chosen toil,
To make the youth of my own island wise."

"I fain would learn the law, or healing art,
And take this northern knowledge o’er the sea,
To serve the humble people of my heart,
And build a happy home where all are free."
No selfish dream inspires his youthful mind,
No thirst for vanity, nor fleeting fame;
A noble soul, in miniature defined,
To bring his distant shore an honoured name.

The fire fades within the iron grate,
The evening bell tolls out its final chime;
I mark the slate whereon his dreams await,
To blossom in the fullness of their time.
Work on, dear child; though fog enshrouds the street,
Heaven preserve the purpose of your youth!
’Tis my sweet task to guide your eager feet
Along the quiet avenues of Truth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short narrative poem about a boy from the West Indies attending a preparatory school in London before going to Westminster.
counterfactuals.output:
In scratchy wool and stiffened lace,
Young Leo treads the foggy square,
A stranger to this frozen place,
With damp air clinging to his hair.
Behind him lie the Tobago shores,
The turquoise swell, the mango tree,
While here, behind heavy oak doors,
He learns the kings of history.

The prep school bell rings cold and clear,
A summons through the London grime;
He learns to hold his tongue in fear,
To march to strict Victorian time.
His fingers ache from Latin prose,
Declining words in drafty halls,
And dream of warmth that no one knows
Beside these high, grey brickwork walls.

On muddy fields, he bowls the ball,
His breath a cloud of sudden white,
And though he stands small-stature, tall,
He harbors sun amidst the night.
They teach him how to play the game,
To speak the language of the realm,
To carve a path, to build a name,
With steady hand upon the helm.

For just across the river’s bend,
Where Abbey towers pierce the slate,
Westminster waits—the planned-for end,
Beyond the heavy iron gate.
There, ancient scholars walk in rows,
Where kings were crowned and poets sleep;
A grander world that calls and grows,
A promise that he swore to keep.

He turns his collar to the rain,
A Caribbean soul in grey,
Accepting cold, enduring pain,
To claim the prize that lies ahead.
With island warmth inside his chest,
He walks beneath the London sky:
A boy from seas of golden West,
Prepared to let his spirits fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write some rhyming verse in an old-fashioned literary voice about a lonely student from abroad who gets inspired by street performers in England?
counterfactuals.output:
Far from the sunlit shores that gave me birth,
I tread the shadowed stone of Albion’s lane,
A lonely scholar on a chilly earth,
Whose weary heart was matched by autumn’s rain.
Behind my glass, the heavy volumes grew
With formal verbs of an un-native tongue;
No friendly hearth nor kindred soul I knew,
Where pale and melancholy mists were hung.

Driven abroad by walls that pressed too near,
I sought the square beneath the twilight sky,
To lose the quiet sorrow brooding here,
And let the grey-clad city pass me by.
When lo! across the damp and stony pave,
There broke a sound of unexpected cheer—
A fiddle’s lilt, defiant, sweet, and brave,
That pierced the gloom and drew the passer near.

A motley troupe of minstrels stood displayed:
A player with a voice of golden flame,
A jester who in tumbled velvet played,
And sang of joy that bore no country’s name.
With silver string and tossed, enchanting sphere,
They painted light upon the dismal gray;
They struck a chord that banished every fear,
And bade the heavy shadows melt away.

No lexicon could bind their vibrant art,
No stranger’s accent marred the song they wove;
They spoke the timeless language of the heart,
Which turns the cold street to a summer grove.
The gathered ring of strangers grew as one,
Bound by the magic of a wooden bow,
And though above us rolled no sudden sun,
My frozen spirit felt a sudden glow.

No longer exiled in a distant land,
Nor crushed beneath the weight of tome and pen,
I caught the spark that left the player’s hand,
And found my place among the ranks of men.
I sought my quiet room as evening fell,
To write and dream beneath a kindled fire;
For art had cast its sweet, redeeming spell,
And filled my heart with courage and desire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem recounting the story of a West Indian boy's childhood in an English boarding school and his surprising choice of profession.
counterfactuals.output:
He came from salt and bougainvillea bloom,
From Kingstown sun that scorched the midday sky,
Where guava sweet swept through his bedroom room,
And turquoise waves sang softly passing by.
His pockets smelled of nutmeg, tide, and earth,
A boy attuned to warmth and tropical mirth.

Then, packed in trunks with heavy brass and leather,
They sent him far across the ocean's swell,
To learn the secrets of the northern weather,
Beneath an English school’s unyielding bell.
A gothic fortress built of cold grey stone,
Where winter chilled him to his very bone.

They wrapped his limbs in scratchy navy wool,
And taught his tongue the proper way to speak.
While mess-hall plates were laden, bland and full,
Of boiled cabbage, mutton, porridge bleak.
He sat beside the radiator’s coil,
Unused to frost upon the muddy soil.

In chapel pews, he watched his breath take form,
A ghost of vapor rising toward the spire,
And longed for rain that fell as heavy, warm,
Not this dull drizzle born of grey desire.
Yet in the classroom, sharp and quick of mind,
He left the other pupils far behind.

The headmaster foresaw a grand career:
“A brilliant youth! The law will suit him well,
Or medicine—a surgeon with no fear!
Or cricket, how his fast-balls break and swell!”
They drew his future out in ink and line,
A noble path where polished brass would shine.

He nodded, smiled, and kept his counsel deep,
And passed his exams with an easy grace.
He let the school its high ambitions keep,
Then packed his bags and vanished from the place.
He shunned the Inns of Court, the hospital bay,
And turned his back on London’s crowded way.

For where did he bestow his gifted sight?
To no fine desk, nor chamber lined with books—
He bought a coat, and climbed into the night,
Far off the coast where icy water churning breaks.
Upon a desolate, storm-battered crag,
Where Atlantic gales unfurled their ragged flag.

He became a keeper of the granite tower,
A guardian of the treacherous Cornish light,
To trim the wicks through every howling hour,
And turn the giant lens against the night.
The boy who froze within the schoolroom air
Now ruled the wild, tempestuous sea-spray there.

They wondered why a son of sun and palm
Would choose the coldest rock, the lonely height.
They did not see that in the storm’s alarm,
He found the ocean’s beat, the guiding light.
Surrounded by the waves he always knew,
He kept the ships safe as the North wind blew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
